title: Quiz: External Data - Fundamentals
prompt: Test your knowledge of memory sections (.data, .bss, .text), ASCII string literals, pointers, and handling command-line arguments in assembly.

questions.question: Which memory section is used specifically for programmer-initialized, read/write data?
questions.explanation: The .data section contains programmer-initialized data and is read/write memory. The .text section is read-only, and .bss is for zero-initialized data.
questions.hint: Think about where global variables with explicit starting values are stored.

questions.question: In C, where are local (automatic) variables always allocated?
options: In the stack frame for a function
questions.explanation: Local (automatic) variables are always allocated in the stack frame for a function. They are not stored in the .data or .bss sections.
questions.hint: These variables only live for the lifetime of the block of code.

questions.question: When executing `main(int argc, char *argv[])`, which registers hold `argc` and `argv` respectively?
questions.explanation: For main(), argc (the number of arguments) is a 32-bit integer passed in w0, and argv (an array of pointers) is a 64-bit address passed in x1.
questions.hint: The number of arguments is a standard integer, but the array is an address (pointer).

questions.question: Which of the following is typically stored in the `.text` memory section?
questions.explanation: The .text section contains program text (machine code) and read-only, programmer-initialized data such as constants and string literals.

questions.question: How do you denote a character constant directly in assembly syntax?
questions.explanation: In assembly, character constants can be denoted with the character enclosed in single quotes, such as 'Z'.
questions.hint: It uses the same syntax as a single character literal in C.
